weekly.title: The model race is becoming an efficiency race
weekly.intro: This edition updates the frontier-model signal after Anthropic pushed its efficiency story into the everyday Sonnet tier and GitHub distributed that model through Copilot.
weekly.theme: Capability still matters, but the enterprise decision increasingly depends on accepted work per unit of time, tool use, policy, and spend.
watchNext: Independent cost-per-accepted-task measurements for Sonnet 5.5 across representative enterprise workloads.
Whether fewer steps and tool calls persist outside Anthropic and GitHub selected evaluations.
How GitHub enterprise model policies affect rollout consistency, cost, and auditability.
Production evidence for Copilot Managed Runtime isolation, recovery, inventory accuracy, and tenant policy enforcement.

weekly.closing: The cheapest token is not necessarily the cheapest result. The next useful benchmark is the bill for work someone accepts.

stories.title: The office assistant is becoming a managed workload.
stories.summary: Microsoft put persistent agents, generated apps, tenant hosting, identity, governance, and usage billing into one Copilot product story. The new unit of work needs an operator, not just a prompt.
stories.author: Dugi Selmanaj
stories.scenario: Microsoft announced Copilot Home, Code, and Autopilot alongside Copilot Managed Runtime and new FinOps controls for agentic work.

facts.text: Microsoft announced the new Copilot with Home, Code, and Autopilot on 25 September 2026.
Microsoft says Code can build apps, dashboards, automations, and workflows in a sandboxed environment that can be hosted inside a customer tenant.

Microsoft introduced Copilot Managed Runtime in public preview as a Microsoft-hosted environment with Entra identity, tenant policies, governed data access, lifecycle management, and centralized inventory.
Microsoft describes Autopilot as a cloud-hosted agent with its own identity, memory, computer, and workspace; it is scheduled to expand to private preview at the end of September.
Microsoft says Cowork, Code, Autopilot, and frontier-model use will use usage-based billing, with administrator spending policies, model-family controls, and user-visible credit balances.

stories.changed: Microsoft joined four previously separate concerns: creating small applications, hosting their code, running persistent agents, and controlling variable AI spend. The announced product surface gives those workloads tenant identity, governed runtime, inventory, policy, and billing rather than leaving them as isolated chat features.
stories.whyItMatters: A persistent agent or generated internal app behaves more like software than a conversation. It keeps state, calls data and tools, consumes money, and may continue after the user leaves. Putting identity, runtime, inventory, and budgets around it acknowledges the operational work that begins when the prompt ends.
stories.technicalImpact: Platform teams will need an inventory that joins agent identity, code version, connectors, data scope, memory, runtime health, policy, audit events, and spend. Tenant hosting can simplify that stack, but teams still need to test effective permissions, isolation, data retention, failure recovery, and how a human stops or repairs a long-running task.
stories.businessImpact: Knowledge workers may be able to create useful internal tools without waiting for a full application project. That can shorten delivery while shifting cost and risk into a larger tail of small, usage-billed workloads. IT will need ownership, support, retirement, and budget rules before those tools become invisible production systems.
stories.outlook: Conditional outlook: if the previews prove reliable and administrators can see and control the effective identity, data, runtime, and spend boundaries, enterprise copilots may become an application platform for non-developers. If controls are fragmented or generated tools are costly to support, adoption may stall at supervised experiments.
uncertainties: Code, Autopilot, and Copilot Managed Runtime are in staged rollout or preview, so the announcement does not establish production reliability or broad customer adoption.
Microsoft describes inherited governance and tenant boundaries but the cited material does not provide independent isolation tests, incident data, or detailed recovery behavior.
A persistent agent can amplify stale instructions, excessive permissions, or incorrect memory over time even when its runtime is centrally managed.
Usage-based billing exposes spend controls but can also make the cost of long-running work less predictable than a user subscription.
Lowering the barrier to internal application creation can increase the number of unsupported tools, duplicated workflows, and unclear business owners.
stories.analysis: The important launch is not another Copilot tab. Microsoft is packaging the pieces an enterprise needs after an agent becomes persistent: a place to run, an identity, a memory, a policy boundary, an inventory, and a bill. That is the point where an assistant starts looking like infrastructure.

stories.title: The AI control plane now decides what arrives by default.
stories.summary: GitHub added local boundaries for agent-run commands and a global default for future Copilot features. Enterprise AI policy is moving from scattered toggles into a control plane.
stories.author: Dugi Selmanaj
stories.scenario: GitHub released local sandboxing for Copilot app sessions and introduced an enterprise default policy for generally available Copilot features, code review, and MCP servers.

facts.text: GitHub announced local sandboxing in the GitHub Copilot app on 23 September 2026.
Project settings can restrict additional filesystem paths, outbound and local-network access, and availability of Git and GitHub CLI credentials.
GitHub says enterprise-managed settings can make the effective policy more restrictive than the project requests.
GitHub says the sandboxed shell fails instead of running without a sandbox when the operating system cannot enforce the requested policy.
Local sandboxing is off by default, applies to new or restarted local sessions, does not cover cloud or remote-host sessions, and remains in public preview.
GitHub announced a global default policy for eligible generally available Copilot features on 24 September 2026.
Enterprises can set eligible current and future features to enabled, disabled, or delegated to organization administrators; the policy is scheduled to take effect on 22 October 2026.
GitHub says explicit feature decisions and preview opt-ins are preserved, and that the default covers eligible feature controls, Copilot code review, and MCP-server policy.

stories.changed: GitHub added two layers of enterprise control. A local sandbox can constrain filesystem, network, and credential access for agent-run commands. A separate global policy can decide whether current and future eligible Copilot features are enabled, disabled, or delegated to organization administrators by default.
stories.whyItMatters: AI governance fails when every new capability arrives as a separate switch that administrators discover after users do. A default policy answers the rollout question before the next feature appears, while the sandbox answers what an active agent can touch. Together they turn adoption from a sequence of product surprises into an explicit operating decision.
stories.technicalImpact: Treat feature defaults and sandbox rules as versioned policy. Record which layer wins, preserve explicit exceptions, test the effective filesystem, network, and credential boundary, and inventory MCP servers and code-review agents covered by the rollout default. A configured policy is useful only if teams can see and audit the effective result.
stories.businessImpact: Central defaults can reduce administrative drift across large organizations and let security teams choose deliberate opt-in. They can also expand AI access silently if an enterprise selects enabled and stops reviewing future eligible features. The setting becomes a standing risk decision, not a one-time convenience.
stories.outlook: Conditional outlook: if vendors expose consistent, auditable controls across models, agents, tools, and clients, enterprise AI policy may become a real control plane. If eligibility exceptions and product-specific settings remain fragmented, administrators will still need manual inventories to understand what users can access.
uncertainties: Local sandboxing remains a public preview, is off by default, and provides no independent escape-testing results in the cited release note.
The global rollout policy does not take effect until 22 October 2026, so this draft cannot verify its behavior across a real enterprise estate.
Eligibility rules and exceptions can change which controls inherit the default; administrators still need an effective-policy inventory.
Local, cloud, remote-host, app, and CLI sessions have different control paths, which can produce inconsistent protection.
A permissive global default or broadly available Git credentials can turn centralized convenience into a larger blast radius.
stories.analysis: The important change is temporal. Administrators are no longer deciding only what is available today; they are deciding the default answer for features that do not exist yet. That saves work, but it also turns a settings page into future policy.

stories.title: The model race is becoming an efficiency race.
stories.summary: Anthropic extended its 5.5 efficiency push from Opus to Sonnet, while GitHub placed the new model directly into Copilot. The useful contest is moving toward accepted work per unit of cost and time.
stories.author: Dugi Selmanaj
stories.scenario: Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5 with unchanged per-token pricing but provider-reported reductions in tokens, task cost, and completion time; GitHub made it generally available in Copilot.

facts.text: Anthropic released Claude Opus 5.5 on 22 September 2026.
Anthropic lists Opus 5.5 at $4 per million input tokens, $20 per million output tokens, and $0.20 per million cache-read tokens, compared with $5, $25, and $0.50 for Opus 5.
Anthropic reports that Opus 5.5 costs 40% less than Opus 5 on its typical-workload tests and generates output more than 30% faster.
Anthropic says Frontier Design and METR evaluated the model before release and that biology and cybersecurity safeguards route some work through restricted access or another model.
Anthropic states that Opus 5.5 may recognize evaluation settings and that pre-deployment evaluations cannot reliably catch every failure.
Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5 on 28 September 2026 and says it generates output more than 30% faster than Sonnet 5.

Anthropic lists Sonnet 5.5 at the same token prices as Sonnet 5—$2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output tokens, and $0.20 per million cache-read tokens—and reports up to 30% lower cost per task because it typically uses fewer tokens.
Anthropic says Sonnet 5.5 is available through its platform and on Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure.
GitHub announced Claude Sonnet 5.5 as generally available in GitHub Copilot on 28 September 2026, with a gradual rollout across its listed editors, agents, apps, web, CLI, and mobile clients.

GitHub says Business and Enterprise administrators can manage Sonnet 5.5 through the Copilot model policy, and that new models are enabled by default unless the administrator disables the global default or the model.

stories.changed: Anthropic extended its efficiency claim from the premium Opus tier to the everyday Sonnet tier. Sonnet 5.5 keeps Sonnet 5 token prices, but Anthropic reports fewer tokens per task, lower task cost, and faster output. GitHub then made the model generally available across Copilot clients with enterprise model-policy controls.
stories.whyItMatters: The practical model decision is no longer only which system tops a benchmark. Teams increasingly need to know which model finishes an accepted task with the least waiting, tool use, correction, and spend. Putting Sonnet 5.5 into Copilot makes that trade-off available inside existing developer workflows rather than as a separate experiment.
stories.technicalImpact: Evaluate complete tasks at fixed effort settings and record success, retries, tokens, tool calls, latency, safeguard fallbacks, and human correction. Treat model availability as a governed dependency: GitHub administrators can control access, and a gradual rollout means the same organization may temporarily see different options.
stories.businessImpact: A faster general-purpose model at unchanged token prices can still reduce the effective cost of high-volume work if it reliably uses fewer tokens and steps. Procurement should test representative tasks before changing routing or budgets, because the strongest efficiency evidence remains provider-reported.
stories.outlook: Conditional outlook: if independent workload tests confirm lower cost per accepted task, model competition may shift from premium benchmark peaks toward efficient routing between capable tiers. If gains depend on Anthropic-selected evaluations, effort settings, or favorable tool patterns, the operational advantage will be narrower than the launch suggests.
uncertainties: Anthropic reports the speed, token-use, task-cost, benchmark, and alignment comparisons; they are not independent measurements across customer workloads.
Sonnet 5.5 keeps Sonnet 5 per-token prices. The claimed cost reduction depends on using fewer tokens and steps, which may vary by prompt, tools, effort setting, and acceptance criteria.
Anthropic says benchmark scores capture only one part of capability and that Opus 5.5 remains stronger for complex, open-ended work requiring sustained judgment.
GitHub describes a gradual rollout, so general availability does not mean every eligible user receives the model at the same moment.
Default model enablement can broaden access unless administrators disable the global default or the model, making rollout policy part of the cost and risk decision.
Anthropic says no evaluation set catches every failure and applies cybersecurity fallbacks to some higher-risk requests; effective behavior can therefore differ by task category.
stories.analysis: The quiet shift is from buying tokens to buying completed work. Sonnet 5.5 keeps the old token price, yet Anthropic argues that fewer steps make each task cheaper. GitHub distribution turns that claim into an immediate enterprise routing question—but the receipt still needs independent measurement.
stories.sourceNote: Primary-source launch material from Anthropic and GitHub. Performance, task-cost, safety, and early-testing claims remain vendor-reported; this edition does not claim independent production validation.

stories.title: An advisory group can review the result. It cannot control the race.
stories.summary: OpenAI and nine mathematicians established an independent group to advise on mathematical AI results. Its remit is public; its power is limited.
stories.author: Dugi Selmanaj
stories.scenario: OpenAI announced an independent group of mathematicians to advise on reviewing, communicating, and releasing mathematical results produced with AI.

facts.text: OpenAI announced the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence on 21 September 2026.
OpenAI says the group will advise on the significance, review, communication, dissemination, and professional standards of emerging mathematical results.
OpenAI says group members are unpaid, may publish advice, may comment without being asked, and control their own membership.
OpenAI explicitly says the group will not advise the company on how to pace its internal progress in mathematics.

stories.changed: A named external group now has a public mandate to advise OpenAI on mathematical AI results and to publish its advice. The group can challenge how results are reviewed and released, but it has no stated decision right over OpenAI's research pace or releases.
stories.whyItMatters: A mathematical proof is not useful because a model produced it; it becomes useful when experts can inspect it, resolve gaps, assign credit, and communicate it without flooding the field. The group creates a place for that work. Its lack of decision power also makes the boundary visible: advice can improve release practice without governing the company that controls the model.
stories.technicalImpact: A credible review process needs stable artifacts: the exact proof, model and prompt context, revision history, reviewer comments, dependency checks, and a record of unresolved objections. Without that package, experts are reviewing a moving claim rather than a reproducible result.
stories.businessImpact: Organizations using AI for high-value research will need domain review capacity, publication rules, and clear ownership of errors. A provider-appointed advisory channel can help, but buyers should still ask who can delay a release, require more evidence, or disclose disagreement.
stories.outlook: Conditional outlook: if the group publishes specific recommendations and OpenAI follows them, domain-led review could become a template for other scientific AI programs. If advice is nonbinding or the underlying artifacts remain inaccessible, the group may add legitimacy without adding much control.
uncertainties: OpenAI reports that its internal model resolved more than 100 long-standing problems, including Navier–Stokes. This draft does not treat those extraordinary capability claims as established facts because independent review is not yet available.
Independence of membership and publication does not create authority over release timing, access to evidence, or company decisions.
The announcement does not yet specify review procedures, disclosure rules, conflict handling, response deadlines, or what happens when OpenAI rejects advice.
stories.analysis: The important announcement is not the large number in OpenAI's capability claim. It is the attempt to build a review institution before those claims arrive at scale. The honest footnote is already present: the institution can advise, and the company still decides.

stories.title: RetroChimera makes chemist judgement part of the test.
stories.summary: A new retrosynthesis system combines two different model types and asks expert chemists whether the proposed routes make sense. That is better evidence, with a small but important caveat.
stories.author: Dugi Selmanaj
stories.scenario: Microsoft Research and collaborators published RetroChimera, a retrosynthesis model evaluated on benchmarks, proprietary pharmaceutical data, and expert chemist preferences.

facts.text: Nature published the RetroChimera paper on 21 September 2026.
The system combines a Transformer-based de novo model and a graph-neural-network template model with a learned ranking strategy.
The paper reports experiments on rare reactions, distribution shift, and transfer or fine-tuning with internal datasets from two pharmaceutical companies.
Microsoft reports that expert chemists accepted RetroChimera routes for nine of ten challenging targets, compared with five, four, and two targets for three comparison systems.
Microsoft released the implementation and weights and links them from its research announcement.

stories.changed: RetroChimera combines two models that fail differently, then ranks their proposals together. The release adds a peer-reviewed paper, expert preference tests, transfer experiments with pharmaceutical datasets, and public code and weights.
stories.whyItMatters: Retrosynthesis benchmarks can reward a prediction that resembles recorded data without proving that a chemist would trust the full route. Adding blind expert judgement moves the test closer to the real decision: is this route plausible enough to spend laboratory time on? The open artifacts also give other researchers a chance to find where that judgement breaks.
stories.technicalImpact: The architecture treats model disagreement as useful information. A flexible generator can suggest unfamiliar reactions while a template model anchors predictions in known patterns; learned voting decides when to trust each. Production use still needs literature checks, feasibility models, uncertainty handling, and prospective laboratory validation.
stories.businessImpact: Better route ranking could reduce the expert time spent triaging impossible options in drug and materials research. It does not remove the expensive part: purchasing inputs, running reactions, measuring yield, and deciding whether a route is safe and scalable.
stories.outlook: Conditional outlook: if independent teams reproduce the results and prospective laboratory studies confirm the proposed routes, chemist-aligned evaluation could become more important than leaderboard accuracy for synthesis-planning tools. The present evidence does not yet show faster or cheaper molecule production in routine use.
uncertainties: The reported whole-route comparison covers ten challenging targets. Nine accepted routes is encouraging, but the sample is too small to establish broad reliability.
Expert acceptance is not the same as successful laboratory synthesis, yield, safety, cost, or manufacturability.
The strongest checkpoint uses licensed Pistachio reaction data through 2023, and performance may fall for newer or substantially different chemistry.
Several authors and the release are affiliated with Microsoft, which developed and distributes the model.
stories.analysis: The useful shift is from ‘Did the model recover the dataset answer?’ to ‘Would a chemist act on this route?’ RetroChimera gets closer to that question. Ten targets still leave a very large laboratory door to walk through.
